**Most impactful problem – the ticket‑scoring values are never defined**

> “Shuffle the tickets and deal 4 cards to each player. … Any returned cards are shuffled together and put at the bottom of the ticket deck …”  
> …  
> “Players reveal all tickets they kept. The value of successfully completed tickets is added to their total score. The value of any incomplete tickets is deducted from their total score.”  

The rulebook never explains **how many points each ticket is worth** (or how negative points are calculated for failed tickets). The only place ticket points appear is in an example (“Blue managed to complete both the ‘Montréal – Atlanta’ and ‘New York – Atlanta’ tickets, adding 15 points…”) but there is no general rule stating, for instance, “each ticket shows its point value on the card” or “ticket values range from 1‑20 points as printed on the card”.  

**Impact**  
Without a rule that tells players what a ticket’s point value is, the final scoring step cannot be performed reliably. Players cannot know whether keeping a risky ticket is worth the potential penalty, and the game’s central mechanic (balancing route building against ticket completion) collapses. This omission makes the game unplayable in practice, as the final scores cannot be calculated.  

*Fix suggestion*: Add a rule such as: “Each ticket card displays a point value in the upper‑right corner. When the game ends, add the displayed value for each completed ticket and subtract the same value for each uncompleted ticket.” This single clarification restores the ability to score the game correctly.

lvl0.2:
**Most impactful problem – ambiguous / over‑restrictive rule for the Longest‑Path bonus**

> “When evaluating and comparing path lengths, **only take into account continuous lines of plastic trains of the same color**.  
> A continuous path may include loops, and pass through the same city several times, but a given plastic train may never be counted twice in the same continuous path.”  

**Why this matters**

The official “Ticket to Ride” rules (on which this game is clearly based) count a longest continuous path **regardless of colour** – any of a player’s trains may be used in the same path. By restricting the path to a single colour:

1. **Extreme imbalance** – A player who secures a long, high‑value colour early (e.g., blue) can easily out‑score everyone else on the 10‑point bonus, while opponents are forced to build a separate mono‑coloured network that is often much shorter.  
2. **Strategic distortion** – The incentive to diversify colours (to claim routes of many colours) disappears; players will race to monopolise one colour, which can dominate the game and make other mechanics (ticket completion, route claiming) secondary.  
3. **Potential for a “runaway leader”** – Once a player has a long same‑colour chain, opponents have little realistic chance to contest the bonus, leading to a predictable outcome and reducing replay value.

Because the longest‑path bonus is worth a flat 10 points (the same as a 6‑space route) and can be decisive in close games, this mis‑statement can give an overwhelming advantage and fundamentally change the game’s balance. The rule should either be removed or corrected to match the standard rule: *count any colour of a player’s trains when measuring the longest continuous path.*

- **Setup (initial tickets)**

- **Draw Tickets action (later in the game)**

These two statements give different mandatory minima for the same type of action (keeping tickets).

- Conversely, the stricter “keep 2” rule at setup forces players to accept potentially very low‑value or even negative tickets right at the start, putting them at a disadvantage before the game even begins.  

The inconsistency creates a loophole that can be exploited for an overwhelming advantage (by repeatedly drawing tickets and discarding all but one), and it also leads to confusion about the correct rule to follow. The rulebook should be unified – either require a minimum of 2 tickets for **all** ticket draws, or specify that the initial draw is the only time the higher minimum applies.

> **“You may have any number of cards in your hand at any time.”**  
> (section *Draw Train Cards*)

**Impact**

Ticket‑to‑Ride’s balance relies on the 12‑card hand limit. Removing that limit lets a player draw and keep every train card they can, stockpiling huge sets of colors (or locomotives). This creates two serious issues:

1. **Overwhelming advantage** – A player who manages to hoard the majority of a color can later claim many long routes in a single turn, gaining a huge point swing that other players cannot realistically counter.

Both effects break the intended flow and fairness of the game. Adding the standard 12‑card hand limit (or another reasonable cap) is necessary to restore balance and prevent a player from gaining an unassailable lead or causing the game to grind to a halt.

lvl1.1:
**Most impactful problem – an impossible “draw tickets” action when the ticket deck is empty**

- **Rule that creates the conflict**  
  > “You can use your turn to draw more tickets. To do so, draw **3 tickets** from the top of the ticket deck. If there are fewer than 3 tickets left in the deck, only draw the ones that are available. **You must keep at least 1 of the tickets you just drew**. Any returned tickets are placed at the bottom of the ticket deck in any order you want.”  

- **Why it is a problem**  
  When the ticket deck has been exhausted (0 tickets remaining) a player who chooses the “draw tickets” action would draw **no tickets**. The rule then forces the player to “keep at least 1 of the tickets you just drew,” which is impossible because there are none to keep. The rule gives no alternative (e.g., “if no tickets are available, you may not take this action”).  

- **Impact on gameplay**  
  1. **Dead‑lock possibility** – Late in the game the ticket deck can run out while some players still have cards in hand and still need to take actions. If a player wishes (or is forced by strategy) to use the “draw tickets” action, they cannot legally fulfill the “keep at least 1” requirement, making the action illegal.  
  2. **Game‑halting** – If all remaining players have no tickets left to draw and also have no viable alternative actions (e.g., they have no train cards to claim routes and the train deck is also empty), the game could stall because the only remaining legal action is blocked by this contradictory rule.  
  3. **Unbalanced advantage** – A player who happens to run out of tickets early loses the option to draw tickets altogether, while others who still have tickets can continue to refresh their hand, creating an unintended advantage.

**Suggested fix** – Add a clause such as:  
> “If the ticket deck is empty, the ‘draw tickets’ action may not be taken.”  
or modify the existing rule to read:  
> “If there are no tickets left to draw, you may not take the ‘draw tickets’ action.”  

This resolves the inconsistency and prevents a potential game‑ending deadlock.

**Most impactful problem – contradictory rule about how many train cards a player may draw in one turn**

- **Turn‑action list (near the start of the “The game turn” section):**  
  > “On your turn, you must perform 1 (and only 1) of the following 3 actions:  
  > 1. **Draw up to 7 train card**”

- **Detailed “Draw Train Cards” rules (later in the same document):**  
  > “You can use your turn to draw train cards. **If you do, you may draw 2 of them.** Either of these cards can be drawn from the 5 face‑up cards …”

These two statements directly conflict: the first tells players they may draw *as many as seven* cards in a single “draw cards” action, while the detailed rules restrict the draw to *exactly two* cards (with the special locomotive restriction).

- **Game balance:** Allowing a player to draw up to seven cards each turn would let them amass a huge hand very quickly, making it far easier to claim long, high‑value routes and to complete tickets. Players who discover or exploit the “7‑card” interpretation would gain an overwhelming advantage, effectively breaking the intended strategic balance of the game.
- **Gameplay flow:** If a player draws seven cards, the “face‑up” replacement rule (draw a card, then immediately replace it) would need to be applied seven times, dramatically speeding up the turnover of the face‑up pool and potentially exhausting the deck far faster than the rules anticipate.
- **Rule ambiguity:** Players and judges will be uncertain which rule to follow, leading to disputes and inconsistent play.

**Resolution needed:** The rulebook must clearly state the correct number of cards that can be drawn in a “draw train cards” action (most likely “draw **2** cards,” as in the original *Ticket to Ride* rules) and adjust the turn‑action list accordingly. Until this is fixed, the game’s core mechanic is ambiguous and can be abused.

lvl4.1:
**Most impactful problem – an over‑powered “search‑for‑locomotive” rule**

> **Draw Train Cards** – “Instead of drawing any of the two cards you can instead reveal cards from the top of the train deck until you reveal a locomotive card. Add the locomotive card to your hand and shuffle the revealed cards with the rest of the train deck.”  

**Why this is a serious issue**

1. **Unbalanced advantage** – A player can spend a turn simply “searching” the deck until a locomotive appears, guaranteeing a wild card every turn without discarding any cards. Locomotives are the most valuable resource for claiming high‑value routes; having a free locomotive each turn makes it far easier to claim long, high‑scoring routes and to complete tickets, overwhelming opponents.

2. **Contradicts the normal draw mechanic** – The rest of the draw‑card rules state that a player may draw **up to two** cards, either from the face‑up pool or blind from the top of the deck, and that a face‑up locomotive must be taken as the first card and then the turn ends. The “reveal‑until‑locomotive” option sidesteps those limits and the “first‑card‑must‑be‑locomotive” restriction, creating an inconsistency in how drawing works.

3. **Potential to stall the game** – Because the revealed non‑locomotive cards are shuffled back into the deck, the deck’s composition never changes, so the player can repeat this action indefinitely. If every player adopts this strategy, the train‑card supply is never depleted, and the game can drag on with little meaningful interaction.

**Result** – The rule as written gives any player a near‑automatic source of wild cards, breaking the intended balance of the game and allowing that player to dominate scoring through routes and tickets. It should be removed or replaced with the standard Ticket‑to‑Ride rule: a player may draw at most two cards per turn, and a locomotive drawn from the face‑up row counts as one of those two draws.

**Most impactful problem – the ticket‑scoring rules are missing.**  

The rulebook tells you how to draw and keep tickets, and it says that at the end of the game “the value of successfully completed tickets is added to their total score. The value of any incomplete tickets is deducted from their total score,” but it never tells you **how many points each ticket is worth** (or how the penalty for an un‑completed ticket is calculated).  

> *“Players reveal all tickets they kept. The value of successfully completed tickets is added to their total score. The value of any incomplete tickets is deducted from their total score.”*  

Because the point values are never defined, players cannot:

1. **Determine the winner** – the final tallies are impossible without knowing each ticket’s score.  
2. **Make informed decisions** when drawing or discarding tickets, since they have no way to weigh the risk/reward.  

Without this essential information the game cannot be played to a conclusive end, making the omission the most severe inconsistency in the rulebook. (All other rules are either self‑consistent or have minor ambiguities.)  

**Recommendation:** Add a table (or list) that specifies the point value for each ticket (e.g., “2‑city tickets: 5–20 points; 3‑city tickets: 7–22 points; etc.”) and state that the same value is subtracted if the ticket is not completed. Once this is included, the rules are complete and the game can be scored correctly.
lvl4.3:
**Most impactful problem – a possible dead‑lock where a player has no legal action**

> *“In the unlikely event that there are no cards left to draw and there is no discard pile, a player cannot take the ‘draw train cards’ action. Instead they may only take the ‘claim 1 route’ or ‘draw tickets’ actions.”*  

> *“To do so, draw 3 tickets from the top of the ticket deck. If there are fewer than 3 tickets left in the deck, only draw the ones that are available.”*

**Why this matters**

If the train deck **and** the discard pile are empty **and** the ticket deck has been exhausted, a player who also cannot claim any route (e.g., lacks the required train cards or does not have enough plastic trains left for any open route) would have **no legal action** available. The rules give no fallback option for such a situation, so the turn cannot be taken and the game can stall indefinitely. This dead‑lock can prevent the “final turn” trigger from ever occurring and leaves the game without a resolution.  

**Impact**

- The game could end prematurely (if players simply stop) or never finish (if they wait for a legal move that does not exist).  
- It gives an unintended advantage to players who manage to deplete the decks early, potentially forcing opponents into a stand‑still.  

**Recommendation**

Add a rule that, when a player has no possible “claim route” or “draw tickets” action because the ticket deck is empty, they may **pass** their turn (or perform a defined “draw from discard” or “re‑shuffle” action). This ensures the game always progresses to its official end condition.
lvl4.4:
**Most impactful problem – contradictory rule about drawing a face‑up locomotive**

> **Rule in “Draw Train Cards” (first paragraph)**  
> “You can … draw 2 … cards. Either of these cards can be drawn from the 5 face‑up cards … or from the top of the deck (a blind draw).”  

> **Later in the same section**  
> “*If you want to draw a face‑up locomotive, it must be the first train card you draw this turn and you cannot then draw a second card.*”

These two statements cannot both be true.  
- The first rule says a player may draw any two cards (including two face‑up cards, or a face‑up locomotive plus another card).  
- The later rule imposes a special restriction that, **only if the first card drawn is a face‑up locomotive, the player may not draw a second card at all**.

Because the rules are ambiguous about what a player may do when a face‑up locomotive is available, players can end up with inconsistent interpretations (some allowing a second draw, others not). This directly affects the core action of the game—drawing train cards—so it can give an unintended advantage (or disadvantage) to players who interpret the rule in the more permissive way, and it can cause disputes that halt play. Resolving this conflict (e.g., by stating clearly whether the “no second draw” restriction applies, or removing it) is essential for the game to function smoothly.
